indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.sub_strand: Data Collection, Organisation, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.1.2 Construct and interpret concrete graphs and pictographs to solve problems
indicator.objective: Draw and interpret concrete graphs and pictographs to solve problems

skills.description: Identify common features of bar graphs (title, labeled axes, key/legend).
Draw a pictograph with one-to-many correspondence.
Solve problems (how many altogether, comparing, take apart) using pictographs.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Ignoring the key when interpreting one-to-many pictographs.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a title on a graph?
options: To tell what the graph is about
questions.explanation: The title tells what the graph is about.

questions.stem: A pictograph uses 1 star for 1 pupil. If there are 6 stars for 'Maths', how many pupils like Maths?
Which of these is a common feature of a bar graph?
questions.explanation: Labelled axes and a title are both features.

questions.stem: A pictograph shows 3 apples for Monday and 5 apples for Tuesday. How many apples in total?
Draw a pictograph to show: 4 boys and 2 girls. Use 1 circle for 1 person.
questions.explanation: The learner should draw 4 circles and 2 circles with labels.

questions.stem: A pictograph shows 1 symbol = 2 pupils. If there are 5 symbols for 'Reading', how many pupils?
A pictograph shows 1 star = 5 books. There are 4 stars for Monday and 2 stars for Tuesday. How many books were read on Monday?
Draw a pictograph to show 10 books. Use 1 book symbol for 2 books.
questions.explanation: The learner should draw 5 book symbols.

questions.stem: A pictograph shows 1 apple = 3 apples. There are 4 symbols for Monday. How many apples?
Explain what a key in a pictograph is used for.
hints: It tells you what one symbol represents.
questions.explanation: A key tells you what each symbol or picture stands for in the graph.

criteria.description: States it tells the value of a symbol.

questions.misconception: Thinking the key is just decoration.

questions.stem: A pictograph shows: 1 symbol = 4 cars. Red has 2 symbols, Blue has 3 symbols. How many more blue cars than red?
A pictograph shows 1 symbol = 10 pupils. If there are 6 symbols, how many pupils?
A pupil wants to draw a pictograph for 30 pupils where 1 symbol = 10 pupils. How many symbols should they draw?
A pictograph has a key: 1 star = 5 pupils. If there are 3.5 stars, how many pupils?
questions.explanation: 17.5 pupils (which might mean the data is represented differently, but mathematically it's 17.5).

questions.stem: Explain how to find the total number of items from a pictograph with a key.
questions.explanation: Count the number of symbols for each category, then multiply by the value of one symbol (given in the key), and add them all together.
questions.misconception: Adding the symbols without multiplying by the key.

questions.stem: List the features of a well-drawn bar graph.
questions.explanation: Title, labelled axes, consistent scale, and bars of correct height.

questions.stem: A pictograph uses 1 circle = 3 pupils. There are 4 circles for 'Maths' and 2 circles for 'English'. How many pupils like Maths or English?
Draw a pictograph with a key of 1 symbol = 2 items for the data: 8 cats, 6 dogs.
questions.explanation: The learner should draw 4 cat symbols and 3 dog symbols, with a key.

questions.stem: A pictograph shows 1 symbol = 5 birds. If there are 4.5 symbols for 'Sparrows', how many sparrows? Explain.
questions.explanation: 4.5 x 5 = 22.5 sparrows. Since you can't have half a bird, the graph might represent an average or the key might be different, but mathematically it's 22.5.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.sub_strand: Data Collection, Organisation, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.1.1 Collect first-hand data and organise it using tallies, checkmarks, charts, lists or line plots to answer and pose questions

skills.description: Use tally marks and checkmarks to collect data, grouping by 5s.
Organize data into frequency tables or lists.
Answer and justify answers based on organized data.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.

questions.stem: How many items are represented by these tally marks: ||||?
hints: Count the marks one by one.
questions.explanation: There are 4 tally marks, representing 4 items.
questions.misconception: Saying 5 because they expect a group of 5.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows: Apples (4), Oranges (6). Which fruit is more popular?
questions.explanation: Oranges (6) are more popular than Apples (4).
questions.misconception: Saying Apples because it comes first.

questions.stem: How many items are represented by these tally marks: ||||/ ? (Note: the / crosses the four lines)
hints: A group of 5 is drawn with a diagonal line across 4 vertical lines.

questions.stem: Data shows: Red (5), Blue (3), Green (2). How many people chose Red?
What is the total number of items if the data is: A(2), B(4), C(1)?
A list shows the number of pets: Dog (4), Cat (3), Fish (2). How many more dogs than fish are there?
Use tally marks to show the number 8.

criteria.description: Draws a group of 5 (with a diagonal line).

questions.stem: A survey shows: Football (6), Netball (4), Athletics (2). What is the total number of pupils surveyed?
A frequency table shows: Monday (5), Tuesday (3), Wednesday (6). On which day was the count highest?
questions.misconception: Saying Monday because it comes first.

questions.stem: Organize this data into a frequency table: 3 pupils like apples, 5 like bananas, 2 like oranges.
hints: Create a column for fruit and a column for number.

criteria.description: Creates a table with correct labels.

questions.stem: A tally chart shows: Cats (||||), Dogs (||||/), Birds (|||). How many dogs are there?
A pupil records data with checkmarks. There are 7 checkmarks for 'Red'. How many items is this?
A frequency table shows: Bus (10), Car (5), Walk (8). How many pupils use transport (bus or car)? Explain.
A tally chart has groups of 5. If there are 3 groups of 5 and 2 extra marks, what is the total count?
Explain why we group tally marks in 5s.
hints: How easy is it to count many marks?
How many marks are in a group?
questions.explanation: Grouping in 5s makes counting faster and easier, especially for large numbers.
questions.misconception: Thinking it's just a rule with no reason.

questions.stem: Data: Team A scored 15, Team B scored 10, Team C scored 8. How many more points did Team A score than Team C?
Create a frequency table for this data: 5 pupils have birthdays in January, 3 in February, and 6 in March.

criteria.description: Creates a table with months and numbers.

questions.stem: A pupil draws 15 tally marks. How many groups of 5 will they have?
A tally chart shows: Red (||||/ ||), Blue (||||/), Green (||||/ |||). How many more Green than Red are there?
questions.explanation: Green (8) - Red (7) = 1. Wait, let me recalculate. Red = 7, Green = 8. 8 - 7 = 1. Let me re-read: Red is ||||/ || which is 5+2=7. Green is ||||/ ||| which is 5+3=8. 8-7=1. I made a mistake in the question logic. Let me change the question to ask for the difference between Green and Blue. Green=8, Blue=5. 8-5=3.

questions.stem: A shop records sales: Monday (12), Tuesday (8), Wednesday (15). Explain how to find the day with the most sales.
questions.explanation: Look at the numbers for each day. The highest number is Wednesday (15), so that is the day with the most sales.
questions.misconception: Saying Monday because it's the first day.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.content_standard: Not clearly printed for this indicator (likely B3.3.3.3)
indicator.objective: E.g.2.Ask learners to say the rhyme Thirty- days has September

skills.description: Use the rhyme to state the number of days in a given month.
Read dates and identify days/months before or after a given date.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Forgetting the leap year rule for February.

questions.stem: How many days does September have?
How many days does January have?
How many days in February in a normal year?
Which month has 28 or 29 days?
Which month comes after March?
hints: March is the 3rd month, so the next is the 4th.

questions.stem: How many days in a leap year February?
Which of these months has 31 days?
hints: 30 days has September, April, June, and November.

questions.stem: If today is 5th June, what date is tomorrow?
How many months in a year have 30 days?
What month comes before December?
Explain how to use the rhyme to remember the days in each month.
questions.explanation: Recite 'Thirty days has September, April, June, and November. All the rest have 31, except February alone...'
questions.misconception: Thinking the rhyme is not useful.

questions.stem: If today is 30th April, what date is tomorrow?
hints: April has 30 days, so tomorrow is 1st May.

questions.stem: A pupil says 'There are 30 days in November.' Is this correct?
hints: 30 days has September, April, June, and November.

questions.stem: List the months that have 31 days.
questions.explanation: January, March, May, July, August, October, December.

criteria.description: Lists most of the correct months.

questions.stem: How many days from 1st to 15th of a month?
A leap year occurs every how many years?
hints: Leap year adds a day to February.

questions.stem: Explain why February has 29 days in a leap year.
questions.explanation: Leap years occur because Earth's orbit takes about 365.25 days. The extra day is added to February every four years.

questions.stem: If today is 28th February in a leap year, what date is tomorrow?
Explain the difference between a normal year and a leap year.
questions.explanation: A normal year has 365 days and February has 28 days. A leap year has 366 days and February has 29 days.
questions.misconception: Thinking leap year adds a day to December.

questions.stem: How many days are there in the first quarter of a non-leap year? (Jan, Feb, Mar)
questions.explanation: 31 + 28 + 31 = 90? Wait, 31+28=59, 59+31=90. So 90. Let me recalculate: 31+28+31 = 90. So answer is 90. I mistakenly wrote 89. Let me correct: 90 days.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.content_standard: B3.3.3.3 Demonstrate an understanding of time taken by events in days, weeks and months
indicator.objective: Use arbitrary units to measure time taken to complete simple events.

skills.description: Measure time using arbitrary units (claps, water timers).
Identify activities that take minutes, hours, days, months, or years.
Determine the duration of an event given start and end times.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Thinking all activities take an hour.
Incorrectly subtracting start time from end time.

questions.stem: Which of these is an arbitrary unit of time?
questions.explanation: A clap is an arbitrary unit.

questions.stem: Which activity takes about 1 minute?
Which activity takes about 1 hour?
A pupil claps 10 times to measure the time to walk across the room. If they clap 20 times to walk back, how many claps in total?
An event starts at 3:00 and ends at 3:30. How many minutes is it?
A pupil uses a water timer to measure time. It takes 2 full timers for an activity. If one timer is 5 minutes, how many minutes is the activity?
Which activity takes about 1 day?
questions.explanation: Both sleeping and a school day are parts of a day, but a full day is 24 hours. Both A and B take place within a day. The question is ambiguous, but 'both' is the best fit.

questions.stem: A film starts at 7:00 PM and ends at 9:00 PM. How many hours is it?
A pupil starts reading at 4:30 and stops at 5:00. How many minutes did they read?
Explain how you could use claps to measure the time it takes to write your name.
questions.explanation: Clap at a steady pace while someone writes their name. Count the number of claps from start to finish.

questions.stem: Which activity takes about 1 year?
Which activity takes about 1 month?
questions.explanation: A school term is about 3 months, but a month is a shorter period. Actually, a school term is longer. A typical month-long activity is a holiday break.

questions.stem: An event starts at 10:15 AM and ends at 11:00 AM. How many minutes is it?
A pupil starts homework at 6:30 PM and finishes at 7:15 PM. How long did it take? Explain.
A pupil uses a pendulum that swings 20 times per minute. If an activity takes 3 minutes, how many swings?
List two activities that take about 1 minute and two that take about 1 hour.
questions.explanation: 1 minute: brushing teeth, tying shoes. 1 hour: a lesson, watching a cartoon.

questions.stem: A journey starts at 9:45 AM and ends at 11:30 AM. How many minutes?
A pupil starts a task at 8:50 AM and finishes at 10:20 AM. How long did it take? Explain your steps.
Explain why arbitrary units like claps are less accurate than standard units like seconds.
questions.explanation: Claps can be fast or slow, so the measurement is not consistent. Seconds are standard and always the same length.

questions.stem: A film starts at 14:30 and ends at 16:15. How long is it?

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.content_standard: B3.3.3.1 Demonstrate an understanding of a metre and centimetre (cm, m) units for measuring length
indicator.objective: Select and justify referents for metre and centimetre

skills.description: Select an appropriate referent for measuring a given object (e.g., a door is about 2 m).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Choosing a referent that is much too small or too large.

questions.stem: Which referent is best for estimating the length of a classroom?
hints: A metre rule is 100 cm long.
questions.explanation: A metre rule is best for large lengths like a classroom.

questions.stem: Which referent is best for estimating the length of a pencil?
questions.explanation: A hand-span is suitable for a pencil.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to estimate the height of a door. Which referent is appropriate?
hints: A door is about 2 metres tall.

questions.stem: Explain why a metre rule is a good referent for measuring the length of a table.
answer: because a table is about 1-2 metres long
a metre rule is about the same size
hints: Compare the size of the table to the metre rule.
questions.explanation: A table is roughly 1-2 metres, so a metre rule is a suitable referent.

questions.stem: Which referent would you use for estimating the thickness of a book?
hints: Thickness is small, measured in cm.
questions.explanation: A centimetre ruler is best for small thicknesses.

questions.stem: A pupil estimates the length of a window using hand-spans. The window is about 3 hand-spans wide. If one hand-span is about 20 cm, what is the estimated width in cm?
Explain why you would not use a hand-span to measure the length of a football field.
hints: A football field is very long.
questions.explanation: A hand-span is too small; you would need too many and it would be inaccurate. A metre rule or tape measure is better.

questions.stem: Which object is about 1 metre long?
hints: 1 metre is about the height of a door handle.
questions.explanation: A door is about 2 metres, but its width is about 1 metre. A desk is usually smaller. A door is the closest.

questions.stem: A pupil uses a 30 cm ruler to estimate the length of a desk. The desk is about 4 rulers long. What is the estimated length?
Explain why a centimetre ruler is a good referent for measuring the length of a pencil.
questions.explanation: A centimetre ruler is about the same size as a pencil, making it a good referent for estimation.

criteria.description: States pencil is about 15 cm long.

questions.misconception: Thinking a metre rule is better.

questions.stem: What referent would you use to estimate the height of a pupil in your class?
questions.explanation: A metre rule or tape measure.

questions.stem: Why is a metre rule better than a hand-span for measuring a door frame?
options: It is more accurate and easier for large lengths.
questions.explanation: A metre rule is more accurate and easier to use for large lengths.

questions.stem: A pupil estimates a table is 2 metres long. If 1 metre is about 3 feet, how many feet is the table?
Explain how you would choose a referent to estimate the length of your classroom.
hints: Consider the size of the classroom.
questions.explanation: A classroom is several metres long, so a metre rule or a tape measure would be a good referent.

criteria.description: Suggests metre rule or tape measure.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to measure the length of a football pitch. Which referent is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A long tape measure is needed.

questions.stem: Explain why we use different referents for different objects.
questions.explanation: Different objects have different sizes. Using an appropriately sized referent makes estimation easier and more accurate.
questions.misconception: Thinking one referent works for everything.

questions.stem: A pupil measures a book with a 15 cm ruler and finds it is 2 rulers long. Then they measure it with a 30 cm ruler and find it is 1 ruler long. What is the actual length of the book?
A pupil says 'I can measure everything with my hand-span.' Explain why this is not true.
hints: Some objects are too big or too small.
questions.explanation: Hand-spans are not suitable for very large objects (like buildings) or very small objects (like a needle). Different referents are needed for accuracy.
